eyebrow: Statistics & Probability for Data Science · Chapter 4, Lesson 15
subtitle: A badly collected sample can be wrong in a way no amount of data fixes.

steps.label: POPULATION -> PARAMETER
steps.sub: Fixed, usually unknown (e.g. true mean spend)

steps.label: SAMPLE -> STATISTIC
steps.sub: Changes from sample to sample -- estimates the parameter

eyebrow: A population we can (for once) see completely
caption: In real work you'd never see this full table -- simulation lets us check our answers.

eyebrow: Five random samples, five different answers
code:
means = [pop["annual_spend"].sample(200, random_state=s).mean() for s in range(5)]
print([round(m, 1) for m in means])
# [169.4, 180.3, 160.6, 162.9, 159.2]
caption: None of these is wrong -- sampling variability. Random error has no systematic lean.

eyebrow: Sampling bias: a systematic tilt, not luck
code:
heavy = pop[pop["orders_per_year"] >= 6]   # only heavy users respond
bs = heavy.sample(n=2000, random_state=1)
print(round(bs["annual_spend"].mean(), 2))   # 241.55 -- true value: 170.22
caption: 2,000 respondents, still badly wrong. 20,000 would just be MORE precisely wrong.

eyebrow: Voluntary response: another flavor of bias
code:
w = pop["annual_spend"] / pop["annual_spend"].sum()
vr = pop.sample(n=2000, weights=w, random_state=2)
print(round(vr["annual_spend"].mean(), 2))   # 250.05 -- ~47% too high
caption: Also watch for survivorship bias (only customers who stayed) and undercoverage.

code:
strat = pop.groupby("region", group_keys=False).apply(lambda g: g.sample(frac=0.002))
print(strat["region"].value_counts().to_dict())
# {'North': 100, 'South': 60, 'West': 40} -- matches population proportions
print(round(strat["annual_spend"].mean(), 2))   # 174.39 -- much closer to 170.22
caption: Guarantees proportional representation -- helps most when groups differ on what you measure.

subtitle: Fix bias with design, not volume. Always ask: who is missing, and why?
